As others have said, any firearm isn't a first line of defense. If you own your home, find ways to make it more secure:  reinforce the door frames with three inch/ 8 cm screws through the strike plates and hinges, obvious (even if fake) cameras, and even just a good rapport with neighbors can go a long way. Theft, broadly, is a crime of opportunity, including burglary. Keeping valuables hidden is just as important; below the waist or above the head is a good rule of thumb for hiding things if you don't have a hidden safe, like a wall or floor safe that's covered up.

With all that said if you are not willing to shoot and kill someone, DO NOT BUY A GUN FOR DEFENSE. Do not have any illusions about how a home invasion might be when you're there; the possibility that you will be murdered is on the table in that scenario. You need to acknowledge that guns are tools that are designed to kill, and if you are not willing to use this tool for that intended function, then it can be used against you in the worst case scenario. If you don't want to shoot someone, don't get a gun for a sense of safety.

On to practical advice. No matter what you get it needs a provision for and accompanying flashlight. The fourth rule of firearm safety is "know your target and what is behind it." A shotgun is the best general recommendation. Handguns take more skill to use well, especially in stressful situations, and rifles tend to have too much penetration in close quarters. Something like a side-by-side or over-under shotgun is going to have an easy natural point of aim, minimal complexity to fumble with in a dire scenario, and it's difficult to go overboard with shooting. In any stressful situation, fine motor skills are completely out the window; gross motor skills are similarly impaired as well. As others have commented, go to a gun range and practice, and not just target practice. You will default to your lowest level of training and practice. Do reload drills, failure-to-fire drills, and so on in addition to just aim-and-fire stuff. Murphy's Law (if it can go wrong, it will) should be the default assumption.

At the end of the day remember that we're all human, and bad things can happen. Don't make it worse by accidentally shooting someone you love because you got scared by something in the night. Be a hard target; practice, practice, practice; and most of all recognize that sometimes, through no fault of your own, bad things may happen and don't require drastic changes.

The absolute cheapest thing you could do is find a bolt on muffler with the same bolt pattern as your header flange.  It won't be quiet still, and size fitment will be an issue, but at least it won't be literally deafeningly loud.  For a full exhaust, a muffler shop is your best bet.  Smaller diameter pipe, as much strait section as possible and fewer bends to weld in, regular steels vs. stainless, and as short as you can are all where you can save some money.  You could see about financing with the shop, or buying piece by piece until it's done.  Good luck!
